chunk_findings.detail:
The new hook status conflates "the stage did not run" with "the stage failed". The surrounding code deliberately distinguishes these: the single-command runner returns `Result(..., reason=p.reason)` at line ~389 for the `not p.ran` case (its own comment at line ~386 enumerates "the runner is missing, the slots are taken, the process did not start"), and only uses a non-zero exit code as "the command's verdict: it ran" (line ~510). `scope.ok["hooks"] = p.ran and p.code == 0` throws that distinction away: a hooks command that never started also yields `False`. The early-return arm then does `if selected: _say_what_ran(scope)`, and `_say_what_ran` scans `order = ("hooks", "selected", "always")`, finds `hooks` present and falsy, and appends "the non-test hooks failed, so the selected tests and the always-run guards did not run". Concrete input: a selected scope whose hooks command cannot start because the runner is missing or the slots are taken (`p.ran == False`, `p.code is None`) — the scope line the gate records now asserts a hooks *failure* that never happened, which is precisely the class of "the line does not say what actually ran" the change is meant to remove. To be correct, the orchestrator needs to record three states (not run / ran-and-failed / ran-and-passed), or `_say_what_ran` must emit "did not run" rather than "failed" when `p.ran` is false.

(No other defect found in the shown hunk; the `asked`/`notrun` computation is consistent with the stage order and the dynamic `scope.ok` keys that are only populated as stages execute.)

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard identifies "is this a bug?" by substring-searching the item's *rendered form* (`out.data["_render"]`), not its kind. Any item whose render happens to contain the letters "bug" is therefore accepted, and `bug show` prints it with exit 0 instead of refusing with "not a bug". The added test only covers `fix-B1`, whose render does not contain that substring, so it passes while the guard is wrong for other inputs. Concretely: create a bug whose text mentions a bug — `ddflow bug found --id B2 --summary "the bug in f returns 1"` — so the auto-created fix task `fix-B2` renders that summary; `ddflow bug show fix-B2` then matches the substring and exits OK printing a *task*, contradicting the command's own contract ("`show`, for a bug only (the id of anything else is refused)"). The check should test the item's kind (e.g. `out.data["_render"] != "bug"`, or the item's kind field) rather than a substring of the rendered output, and the regression test should cover a non-bug whose text contains "bug".

chunk_findings.detail: The change introduces `unran` to distinguish "the stage never started" from "the stage ran and failed", but that distinction is a *local* variable that is only handed to `_say_what_ran`. The new `_scope_evidence` persists the conflated status instead: for a selected scope it does `ev["ran"] = dict(scope.ok)`, and `scope.ok[label]` is `p.ran and p.code == 0`, i.e. pass/fail only. Concretely: hooks pass, the selected test command starts and exits 1 → the recorded scope is `ran == {"hooks": true, "selected": false}`; hooks pass, the selected command cannot start (missing runner / slots taken / process did not start) → the recorded scope is *exactly the same* `{"hooks": true, "selected": false}`. So a consumer that reads this map to say "what actually ran" (the stated purpose of the change, and the substance of the earlier confirmed finding on `scope.ok["hooks"]`) still cannot tell a failed selected run from a selected run that never happened — and will report a stage that ran and failed as "did not run", because the key is named `ran`. The earlier finding is therefore only half-answered: the human-readable `why` line was fixed, but the distinction the fix recovers in `unran` is dropped on the floor before it reaches the recorded evidence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py `_scope_evidence` (new; called at ~L381, ~L390, ~L521)

chunk_findings.detail: `_ci_failed_selected` equates "the item's `ci` gate has `outcome == "failed"`" with "the selected test run was red". Those are not the same on a multi-stage gate, and the accepted earlier finding on this very change establishes that: the surrounding code deliberately keeps `ran=False` distinct from `code != 0`, because a stage can be `failed` without its command ever running (missing runner, taken slots, a hook that could not start), and the `ci` gate aggregates such stages. A gate that failed in one of these ways still carries a recorded `ci_scope` of `{"scope": "selected"}` — that is exactly the situation the bug report describes, where the scope line said "selected 62 files" while something else happened. So for an item whose `ci` gate failed because a non-test stage failed or could not start (or where the selected tests were never the thing that failed), `_ci_failed_selected` returns `True`; `_scope_for` then skips both `_ci_not_passed_here` and `_after_ci` and scopes `unit_tests` to the same narrow selection, with a reason string that asserts "the ci gate FAILED its selected run". The result is that the gate runs only the selection and *claims* a verdict on tests that were never red (in the "did not start" case, never ran at all), while the full-suite fallback whose entire justification is that the `ci` evidence is not a trustworthy verdict here is silently dropped. The fix should key on the reason/`ran`-vs-`code` distinction (as the rest of the file does), not on the gate outcome alone; otherwise the condition fires for inputs the existing code classifies as "the command never ran".

chunk_findings.detail:
The new short-circuit only fires in the "text names no file" branch, so it never applies to a tool bug whose text *does* name files — including the very bug this change is fixing. The recorded text of `Bc0b26248e3` is "…brief lists globs of another fix (claim.py, leases.py)… ddflow brief … fix-B1579b8a1a9 prints 'Globs (the files you may write): ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim.py, ddflow/services/leases.py, tests/test_claim_own_expired.py, …'". The fix task for that bug is filed with `summary` as the `text` argument, so `_PATHISH.findall(text)` is non-empty and the code falls through to `[g for g in source_globs if any(_names(p, g) for p in named)]`. The source item is the one the bug was found on (`fix-B1579b8a1a9`), whose globs *are* the claim-work globs the bug complains about, so the intersection matches `ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim.py` / `ddflow/services/leases.py` and hands exactly those globs back to the fix task. Concretely: `inherit_globs(["ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim.py", "ddflow/services/leases.py"], <Bc0b26248e3 summary>, tool_bug=True)` returns the claim globs, not `[]` — the repro `ddflow brief --for-agent X fix-<new>` still prints "Globs (the files you may write): ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim.py, …". The change only fixes tool bugs filed with a summary that names no path (e.g. a pure prose title); any tool bug whose text quotes the offending file names — which is what a bug report about wrong globs naturally does — keeps the bad inheritance, and a regression test written against the real repro text would still fail.

(Everything else I checked — the `scope or prior.scope or "project"` fallback at the live site, the added keyword-only default so other `_file_fix_task` callers keep working, and the explicit-`--globs` path bypassing `inherit_globs` — is consistent.)

A gate that failed in one of these ways still carries a recorded `ci_scope` of `{"scope": "selected"}` — that is exactly the situation the bug report describes, where the scope line said "selected 62 files" while something else happened. So for an item whose `ci` gate failed because a non-test stage failed or could not start (or where the selected tests were never the thing that failed), `_ci_failed_selected` returns `True`; `_scope_for` then skips both `_ci_not_passed_here` and `_after_ci` and scopes `unit_tests` to the same narrow selection, with a reason string that asserts "the ci gate FAILED its selected run". The result is that the gate runs only the selection and *claims* a verdict on tests that were never red (in the "did not start" case, never ran at all), while the full-suite fallback whose entire justification is that the `ci` evidence is not a trustworthy verdict here is silently dropped. The fix should key on the reason/`ran`-vs-`code` distinction (as the rest of the file does), not on the gate outcome alone; otherwise the condition fires for inputs the existing code classifies as "the command never ran".

chunk_findings.detail: The only end-to-end regression test for this fix files the `--scope ddflow` bug with `summary="no bug show command"` — a report whose text names no file. That is not the scenario of the bug being closed: the recorded text of `Bc0b26248e3` quotes the other fix's files ("…claim.py, leases.py…", the very brief output being complained about), and the previous review's complaint was precisely that the short-circuit only fired in the "text names no file" branch. So the path the user's repro actually takes — `bug_found(..., scope="ddflow")` with a summary that quotes file names, then `brief --for-agent` — is never exercised: if `bug_found` derives `tool_bug` from the text (e.g. only sets it when no file name is parsed) instead of from `scope`, or wires it only in that branch, this test still passes while the brief keeps printing another fix's globs. The same weakness appears in `test_file_tasks_keeps_the_scope_when_it_files_the_task_later`: its single assertion `globs == []` is also the outcome of a deferred-filing path that inherits nothing for *any* bug, so it cannot distinguish "the scope was carried over" from "the deferred path lost the item context entirely"; a companion deferred *project* bug (expecting `SRC`, as the direct path asserts at line 37) is needed to make the claim non-vacuous.
